title: Types of Agents
html:
Agent programs range from simple lookup rules to systems that plan, weigh trade-offs and improve themselves. Each type adds one capability to the previous one.

Agent typeDecides usingStrengthLimitationExample
Simple reflexCondition–action rules on the current perceptFast, simpleFails when the world is partially observable; can loop foreverThermostat, the vacuum agent above
Model-based reflexRules + an internal state updated by a model of how the world evolvesHandles partial observabilityStill has no explicit goalsCar tracking vehicles it can't currently see
Goal-basedA model + goals; searches/plans for action sequences that reach themFlexible — change the goal, not the rulesGoals are binary: all paths to the goal look equally goodRoute planner, puzzle solver
Utility-basedA utility function scoring how desirable each state is; maximises expected utilityTrades off speed, safety, cost; handles uncertaintyUtility is hard to specify; heavy computationSelf-driving car choosing a route
Learning agentAny of the above + components that improve it from experienceWorks in unknown environments; gets betterNeeds data/experience; can learn wrong thingsSpam filter, game-playing RL agent

Why internal state matters

Add a cost of 1 point per move to the vacuum world. The simple reflex agent can't remember that B is already clean, so it shuttles back and forth forever. A model-based agent remembers both squares and stops (NoOp):

Goals vs utilities

A goal-based agent asks “does this reach the goal?”; a utility-based agent asks “how good is this outcome?”. Utility is needed whenever goals conflict (speed vs safety) or success is uncertain — the agent then maximises expected utility (see Utility & Markov Decision Processes).

The learning agent

Performance element

The agent proper — selects actions (any of the four designs above).

Critic

Judges how well the agent is doing against a fixed performance standard and gives feedback (e.g. a reward).

Learning element

Uses the critic's feedback to improve the performance element.

Problem generator

Suggests exploratory actions that lead to new, informative experiences — exploration.

Key point

LLM-based “AI agents” fit this template: the LLM is the performance element choosing actions (tool calls), a memory/scratchpad is the internal state, the user's task is the goal, and feedback loops play the critic. See the Generative AI notes.

When is a simple reflex agent enough?

When the environment is fully observable and the right action depends only on the current percept — e.g. a thermostat. With partial observability it needs internal state (model-based) or it may loop forever.

Why would you prefer a utility-based agent over a goal-based one?

Goals only distinguish success from failure. A utility function ranks outcomes, so the agent can trade off conflicting objectives and weigh the probability of success — essential under uncertainty.
